extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning how to write and read mathematical proofs (introductory 'proofs' / discrete math students)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for constructing common proof forms (biconditionals, conjunctions, disjunctions, existence/uniqueness, elementwise set proofs) including recommended strategies, common pitfalls, and how to write final proofs from scratch work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving a biconditional (P iff Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove P iff Q, prove the two conditionals P -> Q and Q -> P separately (the ‘left-to-right’ and ‘right-to-left’ halves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the two directions as separate goals; you may choose to perform scratch work naming witnesses (like j) but omit such names in the polished final proof if unnecessary. Sometimes the two directions use the same steps in reverse order and can be compressed into a chain of equivalences P iff R iff Q. Do not assert P iff Q until each direction has been justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using existential and universal quantifiers correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: When a given starts with an existential quantifier, instantiate it (choose a witness) immediately; when the goal starts with a universal quantifier, let the variable be arbitrary and prove the remaining statement for that arbitrary element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce names for witnesses (e.g., let x0 be such that P(x0)) by existential instantiation. For universal goals, pick an arbitrary element and work with it, then conclude universal generalization. Rename bound variables when necessary to avoid confusion between free and bound occurrences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling negated goals via contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: If your goal is a negation (¬S) and reexpressing it would rely on the very equivalence you are trying to prove, use proof by contradiction: assume S and derive a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up a contradiction goal and use existing givens to get a contradiction (as in proving ¬∃ leads to assuming ∃ and reaching contradiction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain-of-equivalences shortcut
rubrics_metrics.description: If proofs of P -> Q and Q -> P follow the same reasoning in opposite directions, you may present the result as a string of equivalences P iff R iff Q (an abbreviation for P iff R and R iff Q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to shorten final write-ups: start with equivalences you can justify and string them to reach the goal. Ensure each step asserted in the final string is justified (do not start with the unjustified P iff Q and work backwards).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving set equalities elementwise
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove two sets are equal, either prove Vx(x∈A ↔ x∈B) (elementwise equivalence) or prove the two subset relations A⊆B and B⊆A separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical approach: let x be arbitrary, then show x∈left ↔ x∈right. This often produces an iff-goal that you handle by proving both directions (or by chaining equivalences for x∈ statements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating conjunctions (goals and givens)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the goal is a conjunction (P ∧ Q), prove each conjunct separately. If a given is a conjunction, you can split it into separate givens and use each part where needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the conjunction as two separate goals or givens; it's legitimate to handle them sequentially. In final proofs you may omit some routine justifications but must understand they follow from existential/universal rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by cases from a disjunctive given (P ∨ Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a given has the form P ∨ Q, break the proof into cases: assume P and prove the goal, then assume Q and prove the goal. Because P ∨ Q guarantees one case holds, the goal follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write separate numbered cases in the final proof. Cases must be exhaustive (cover all possibilities) but need not be exclusive (overlap is allowed). Show in each case how the goal follows from that branch's assumptions and other givens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using disjunction to prove a disjunction (P ∨ Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a goal of the form P ∨ Q, you can break into exhaustive cases and in each case prove either P or Q; if in case 1 you can prove P and in case 2 you can prove Q, then overall P ∨ Q holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatively, use the trick: if P is true then P ∨ Q holds immediately; otherwise assume ¬P and prove Q (since P ∨ Q is equivalent to ¬P → Q). This reduces the problem to proving Q under the extra assumption ¬P.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing useful cases (when none are suggested)
rubrics_metrics.description: If no disjunctive given suggests cases, choose cases that simplify the statement (e.g., parity: even vs odd, sign: positive vs nonpositive) — exploratory examples or small trials can suggest the right partition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try a few sample values or examine the algebraic form to see natural dichotomies; the chosen cases must still be exhaustive for all possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disjunctive syllogism (rule of inference)
rubrics_metrics.description: From P ∨ Q together with ¬P (or a proof that P is false) you may conclude Q. Symmetrically, from P ∨ Q and ¬Q conclude P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a standard inference used to simplify proofs when one disjunct can be eliminated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving equalities by expanding and matching
rubrics_metrics.description: For algebraic equalities, compute/expand both sides and show they reduce to the same expression; present a string of equalities starting from one side and ending at the other (possibly by reversing the second computation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let variables be arbitrary if the statement is universally quantified. Use the most straightforward sequence of algebraic manipulations and justify each equality; when two expansions match, conclude equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence proofs (∃! and ∃)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove ∃x P(x), exhibit a particular x (a witness) and prove P(x). For uniqueness (∃!x P(x)), prove existence and then prove that any two objects satisfying P must be equal (VyVz((P(y) ∧ P(z)) → y = z)), or use equivalent formulations like ∃x(P(x) ∧ ∀y(P(y) → y = x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple equivalent logical forms are given; pick the approach that makes the argument easiest (constructive witness for existence; a separate uniqueness argument).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding unjustified backward reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not begin the write-up by asserting the goal P → Q (or P ↔ Q) and then working out meanings to justify that assertion; instead, start with statements you can justify and build up to the goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scratch work may proceed in any convenient direction to discover the proof, but the final presentation must assert only statements that are already justified by prior steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renaming bound variables to avoid confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid confusion between an arbitrary/free variable and a bound variable of a formula, rewrite the bound variable (e.g., change ∃x P(x) to ∃y P(y)) so the roles are clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is recommended when the same symbol would otherwise appear both as the previously 'let arbitrary' element and as a bound variable; it keeps substitution steps clear in the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existential instantiation justification (introducing j,k, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: When you write 'choose an integer k such that 2k = n' from a given '2|n', this step is justified by existential instantiation — you are allowed to introduce such names as witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although polished proofs sometimes omit the explicit justification, you should know that such introductions are justified by the meaning of existential statements; similarly, when proving a conjunct you may implicitly use that the constructed value is an integer (show it or note it as routine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Using contradiction when reexpression is circular
rubrics_metrics.description: When reexpressing a negated goal would rely on the same equivalence you're trying to prove (circular), prefer proof by contradiction: assume the opposite and derive a contradiction using available givens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was demonstrated in showing ∀x ¬P(x) → ¬∃x P(x) style patterns: set up a contradiction table with givens and goals and use instantiation to reach contradiction.
